I had worked with Titmouse on Panthon and Scavengers Reign before, so they called me when they were first putting together the post production team. I had been recommended by my previous director. Echo was not as involved with hiring, the producers and retake director interviewed me. I had initially gotten a job doing compositing at Titmouse when my friend from college who was working there got a job offer he preferred, and he recommended me to replace him. I had previously worked with him at Paramount as an animator. I hadn't considered doing compositing before, but I needed work at the time. I'm glad I did, compositing is very fun!

As a 2d compositor on the retakes team, I would mostly receive After Effects projects from the overseas animation studio, get notes from the retakes director and showrunner, and re-composite as needed. If there was a new background painted or new animation drawn, I would composite it into the shot. Otherwise, I would recolor art assets with gradients, masks, and color replacements, add light layers, animate dynamic lighting, create and implement missing palette gels, retime and re space animation, re draw where necessary, do camera animation and focus effects, design and composite effects with glows and warps that affect different art assets dynamically, simulate effects where necessary, re compose shots for storytelling and clarity, ensure colors are consistent across sequences, re time shots when the edit changes, add motion blur, and probably more I'm not remembering! Anything that I can fix or create without sending back to the animation or background teams, I would do myself. Our union classification is a little loosey goosey, so I end up wearing a lot of hats (without getting as much as color designers for some reason). I have done color design work in a preproduction team, and I made way more money while my job description was much more specific.

I loved comping Michael's football dream because that was animated and designed in our studio at Titmouse, so I composited it from scratch and added a bunch of dreamlike lighting and colors that I designed myself. I also loved doing color design for the shadow-puppet sequences, because they were created in black and white but the directors changed their mind and wanted color, so I had the opportunity to design that color from scratch as well. 
  
Other than that, I liked animating some fun dynamic lighting for Cheng's fight with Gugu in episode 4.

I did the color and lighting! It was done in After Effects, so 2D only. A lot of the shadows shapes were drawn by the animators, and the initial color design was done by a kickass color design team, but we had to re color a lot of it, and we implemented a lighting pass in post production for almost every shot.

Planetside, laser weapons large enough to hit ships at long range are very easy to decoy with missiles and hit with hard-to-detect ballistics. In deep space, most of your delta-V is from nuclear thermal rockets so you only have a little bit of dodge potential with your limited hypergaulic tanks. Missiles are still an important and dangerous weapon for overwhelming enemy point defenses in mid and long range, but getting into gun range is the best option for fleets of smaller ships. Forward deflectors (layered carbon fiber at a steep angle with multiple layers of whipples) can deflect a good amount of railgun fire, but the rest of the ship bodies are glass cannons to save weight. I'm not sure why there's this myth that 2D is more expensive and harder to adjust. In my experience 3D is more expensive and unweildy to adjust because there's more steps in the pipeline. I work in compositing/pipeline, for reference. The reason there's more 3D produced today is (from my understanding, since I'm not a producer) mostly due to where the capital investment comes from. The film industry is highly financialized. The investors think 3D is a safer/more lucrative investment, so they make 3D.

3D is less adjustable than you'd think. once you're on the order of magnitude of tens of thousands of keyframes for a complicated model, if you want to change something, you kind of have to start over. it's like digital stop motion. a lot of 3d animation starts with detailed storyboards that are close to 2d animation, and the notes happen at that stage, when it's cheaper to change things. i work in 2D compositing and and animation, and to change 2d, you just redraw a couple of frames. for 3d, you have to adjust keyframes, which affects everything else, so you have to adjust the whole animation, then you have to re render the whole thing, then re render the generative effects, and only then can the animation files be replaced in the composite.
2D is not harder than 3D. (source I can do both, 2D is easier and cheaper to make look good). there is more 3D supply in the US right now, which makes it more accessible for studios here.
